name: Meaningful Sequence
explanation: When the order in which content is presented affects its meaning — a form's fields, the steps in a process, an article's paragraphs, a multi-column layout that reads top-to-bottom then column-by-column — that reading order has to be something a browser or assistive technology can figure out automatically, not just something that looks right visually. In practice this almost always means: the order elements appear in the HTML (the DOM source order) should match the order a sighted user reads them in. A screen reader, a braille display, and a screen magnifier all rely on source order (or another programmatic order, like CSS Grid's `order` combined with proper structure) rather than on how things are positioned visually with CSS. If CSS is used to visually rearrange content — reversing a flex row, repositioning something with absolute positioning, reordering grid items — without the DOM order matching, sighted users and screen reader users end up experiencing two different, disconnected sequences.
whoItAffects: Screen reader users (JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver) navigate and listen to content in DOM source order, not visual order — if CSS has visually reordered content so it no longer matches the markup, they'll hear a sequence that doesn't make sense, such as an answer being read before its question, or a form's submit button being announced before the fields it submits. Screen magnifier users who zoom in and pan around a page also rely on a logical underlying order as they move focus or scan region by region, since they can only see a portion of the visually reordered layout at once. Switch-access and keyboard-only users are affected too, when tab order (which typically follows DOM order) jumps around in a way that doesn't match what's visually adjacent on screen, making the interface feel unpredictable. People with cognitive disabilities benefit from a reading order that follows a natural, logical progression rather than one that's been visually rearranged in a way that breaks the narrative or logical flow.
howToTest: Turn off CSS in your browser's developer tools (or use a browser extension/reader-mode view that strips styling) and read the page from top to bottom in its now-unstyled, source order. Does that raw order still make logical sense — do headings, paragraphs, form labels/fields, and steps in a process appear in the same sequence a sighted user would naturally read them? If content that visually appeared first (like a summary or a set of instructions) now appears after content it depends on, or a multi-column layout collapses into a jumbled single column, the DOM order doesn't match the meaningful reading order and the page fails this criterion.

check.question: A page uses CSS `flex-direction: row-reverse` to visually swap two side-by-side panels, but doesn't change the underlying HTML order. What is the accessibility problem this creates?
choices: Screen reader users will hear the panels in DOM order, which no longer matches what sighted users see, creating two different sequences
The page will fail to render in older browsers that don't support flexbox
There is no problem, because CSS reordering never affects assistive technology
The panels will become impossible to focus using the keyboard
